Patient Name: Christina Cooper
DOB: 07/01/1954
New patient referred by Diane Nelson for long-standing iron deficiency anemia.

History of Present Illness:
Patient is a new patient seen for long-standing iron deficiency anemia, which she has had since she was 13 years old. She was recently told she was anemic around December when she tried to donate blood. She reports feeling frequently fatigued during the day, feverish with chills at times, and experiences chilling sensations and gets cold easily, requiring her to bundle up. When trying to be active, she feels like she cannot catch her breath, experiences wheezing, and has developed headaches. She also notes that her anxiety and depression have been getting worse lately. She had heavy periods in the past until she had a hysterectomy in 1996, but previous doctors have not told her why she is anemic.

Past History:
Hysterectomy in 1996 for heavy periods.
Last colonoscopy was about 5 to 6 years ago and was reported as normal with no polyps, and she was told to return in 10 years.
No pacemaker, no defibrillator, no sleep apnea, and does not use oxygen at night.
Alcohol use: Once or twice a year.

Current Medications and Supplements:
Ferrous sulfate 25 mg tablets, twice daily (one in the morning, one in the evening). She recently restarted these after not taking them for about a year.
Over-the-counter vitamin B12.

Physical Exam:
General physical exam template used. Heart and lungs auscultated. Abdomen examined with the patient laying back; no tenderness to palpation. Physical exam is normal without any significant findings.

Assessment and Plan:
1. Iron deficiency anemia with symptoms of fatigue, chills, shortness of breath with exertion, wheezing, and headaches. Suspect internal bleeding as an initial possibility.
2. Schedule an upper endoscopy (EGD) and a colonoscopy to assess for potential sources of anemia or GI bleed. Bowel prep instructions provided. Patient has no history of issues with sedation other than being sleepy afterwards.
3. If EGD and colonoscopy are normal, will consider a capsule endoscopy (pill camera).
4. Send a referral to hematologist Dr. Flores for evaluation regarding potential intravenous iron or medication to help store iron better.
5. Instructed patient to take her iron pills (ferrous sulfate 25 mg twice daily) with orange juice (vitamin c helps absorb iron better) for 8 to 12 weeks, after which blood work will be reassessed.
6. Follow-up blood work to include CBC, iron, ferritin, b12, and folate after the 8-12 week trial.
7. Patient advised to call with questions or worsening symptoms.

PATIENT: Bruce Ward
DOB: 5/21/1969
AGE: 52-year-old male
VISIT DATE: Neurosurgery Consultation
REFERRING PHYSICIAN: Dr. Henry Howard
CONSULTING PHYSICIAN: Dr. Flores

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: 
This is a 52-year-old male with a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion, seen in consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for possible surgical intervention. Mr. Ward presented to Dr. Howard on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denied any trouble with headaches in the past. Workup initiated by Dr. Howard included a brain MRI and serology, where a pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered. 

The patient states he is getting fed up with the headaches, which have been going on for months. The headaches are located behind his eyes and are described as a dull, nagging ache. The onset was gradual, starting about three months ago, and they have been getting worse over time. Initially, the severity was about 3 out of 10 and gradually worsened to about 6 out of 10. The headaches tend to be worse in the morning, last a few hours at a time, and nothing makes them better or worse. 

He denies feeling sick, fever, rashes, neck issues, numbness, tingling, or passing out. However, he notes that recently he seems to be bumping into door frames. He has not noticed any change in his vision or balance. His eyes were checked in the fall. He tried Tylenol a few times for the headaches, but it did not work, so he stopped.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: 
Unremarkable. He has no other medical problems and does not take any medicines.

FAMILY HISTORY: 
The patient was adopted, so he has no idea of his family history of diseases.

SOCIAL HISTORY: 
He works as a computer programmer, has been married for 25 years, and they just bought a small house. He does not drink alcohol, smoke, or use recreational drugs, and never has.

REVIEW OF LABS AND RADIOLOGY: 
Personally reviewed labs dated 3/3/21 including CBC, unates (unes), coagulation, and CRP, all of which were normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low TSH; all other results were normal. Personally reviewed pertinent radiology studies including MRI of the brain with contrast from 3/4/21, which reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. The ventricles are normal in size and no other abnormalities are noted.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: 
The patient is alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal, motor, or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
Diagnosis is pituitary adenoma. Mr. Ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has a benign-appearing pituitary adenoma, incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. He is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression; therefore, surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated. 

The mass is a well-defined mass pressing on the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia, which explains why he has been bumping into door frames. The only option to treat this vision loss from mass compression is surgery, specifically a transsphenoidal approach which is minimally invasive and goes through the sphenoid sinus. 

Discussed risks of anesthesia including heart attack, stroke, and death. Discussed risks of surgery including infection, need for further surgery, wound issues such as spinal fluid leak or infection which may require prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure, seizure, stroke, permanent numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking, or death. The removed adenoma will be sent to pathology to confirm the diagnosis.

Plan to refer the patient to an eye doctor for a full exam and a visual field test to map his peripheral or side vision prior to surgery, with monitoring after surgery to see if vision improves. He will see the surgery scheduler, Deborah, on the way out to get the surgery scheduled fairly quickly.

Patient Name: Betty Hill
DOB: 2/21/1968
Past Medical History: Uterine fibroids, anemia, cholecystectomy (gallbladder removed several years ago)
New patient referred from the ER for esophagitis.

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a new patient presenting after an ER visit for chest pain. She states she experienced chest pain for four days in early October 2020. The pain occurred randomly, was located in the center of her chest right behind her breastbone, and felt like a heart attack with a really sharp pain. Nothing she did relieved it, prompting her to go to the emergency room where an EKG and blood tests were performed and were normal. Cardiac workup was normal. 

She notes the pain was worse with eating and she also had difficulty swallowing at the time. Both the chest pain and swallowing problem resolved about three days after she went to the ER (total of about 7 days after onset, three months ago), and she has not had any since. She is unsure if she has ever had heartburn or indigestion. She has been trying to lose weight. She denies abdominal pain and states her bowel movements are normal. She notes she was going through a really stressful job transition right around the time the symptoms happened.

Family History: No known family history of GI problems.
Abdominal Surgeries: Cholecystectomy several years ago.

Physical Exam:
General: Appears well.
Abdomen: Lower belly is soft and non-tender to palpation. Upper abdomen shows mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants, about the same on the left and right. Otherwise, the exam looks normal and good.

Assessment:
Brief summary of patient's history: 52-year-old female with a history of uterine fibroids and anemia, presenting with a resolved, isolated episode of sharp central chest pain and difficulty swallowing occurring three months ago in early October 2020, with a normal cardiac workup in the ER. 
Possible etiologies include GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. 
Suspect she had an anxiety attack related to her job transition, plus or minus a contribution from her musculoskeletal etiologies.

Plan:
- Discussed options including an EGD (upper endoscopy) to look for esophagitis versus continued monitoring for additional symptoms. 
- Patient elected to hold off on the EGD and self-monitor her symptoms, as she has been asymptomatic for three months and any potential esophagitis would likely be healed by now. 
- Patient will call the office if she has any additional episodes of pain, reoccurrence, change, or any other symptoms she is concerned about, at which point an EGD can be scheduled. 
- Patient will follow up as needed for any other GI complaints.

She notes a little bit of tingling, though she cannot tell if it is due to the swelling, and she can still feel her fingers. She applied ice, used an ace wrap at home, and took ibuprofen, which helped a little bit. She has no prior history of injury to this arm. Pain is worse with movement in any direction and is somewhat better when kept straight around a regular level on a pillow. 

Review of Systems:

- Cardiovascular: Heart rate regular, no murmur, no rub, no gallop.
- Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
- Extremities: Lower legs have palpable pulses, no lower edema. Upper extremities show normal range of movement in shoulders. Right wrist exam notable for tenderness on palpation on the inside and outside, pain on flexion, extreme difficulty with extension, pain with radial and lateral deviation, and inability to make a tight fist. Vitals:

- Heart Rate: 80 beats per minute
- Temperature: 97.2 degrees Fahrenheit

Assessment and Plan
1. IgA Deficiency: Confirmed by recent lab work showing a low immunoglobulin A level. This is a common immunodeficiency. Most people live their entire lives without knowing they have it and function normally. Some people get frequent respiratory tract, sinus, or abdominal infections, which does not appear to be the case for this patient. Low likelihood of other associated immunodeficiencies, but additional blood work will be ordered to check other antibodies.

3. Next Steps: Order additional blood work to check other antibodies and bring the patient in for those labs.

REASON FOR VISIT: Evaluation of right elbow pain.

The pain keeps him up at night and makes it difficult sometimes to lift and do things, though he tries to work through it. He has tried ibuprofen, which helps a little but not much.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: 
Vitals look good. 
Focused exam of the right elbow: 
- Positive for pain to palpation with moderate tenderness of the medial epicondyle.
- Turning wrist like turning a doorknob: Not really any pain.
- Turning wrist in (pronating the forearm): Positive for pain.
- Raising hand by bending at the wrist against resistance: Positive for pain with resistance against flexion of the wrist.

IMAGING: X-ray of the elbow shows no fracture or bony abnormality of the right elbow.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:

- Apply ice to the elbow for 20 minutes, 3 times a day.
- Ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food for a full week.
- Hold off on doing any type of pottery work for the next couple of weeks.
- Return for follow-up in one week to see how he is doing.

SUBJECT: Russell
CHIEF COMPLAINT: Sharp pain on the right side of the abdomen below the ribs for the last several days.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient states he saw his primary care doctor who ordered a CT scan, stated he had a kidney stone, and sent him to see the urologist. The pain goes to his lower abdomen and into his groin. The pain comes and goes; when it comes, it is pretty bad and he feels like he cannot find a comfortable position. He reports mild burning when he urinates. He does not think there is any frank blood, but his urine looks a little dark sometimes. He has taken some Tylenol, but it has not really helped. He feels nauseated, but is not vomiting. He denies fever and chills.
FAMILY HISTORY: Father had kidney stones.
PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Previous kidney stones that he has been able to pass, but this one is taking a lot longer.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Abdomen: No tenderness to palpation, no evidence of any rebound or guarding, no peritoneal signs.
Flank: Positive CVA tenderness on the right flank, indicating tenderness over the right kidney and potential inflammation.
REVIEW OF IMAGING: CT scan of the abdomen ordered by the primary care doctor shows a 0.5 cm kidney stone located in the proximal right ureter. There is no evidence of hydronephrosis (swelling of the kidney).
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Acute nephrolithiasis (kidney stone).
- Push fluids to help facilitate urination and peeing to help pass the stone.
- Prescribed oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours as needed for pain. Can continue to alternate with Tylenol.
- Provided a strainer to use for straining urine to catch the stone when it passes for testing.
- Ordered a basic metabolic panel, urinalysis, and urine culture.
- Follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks. If still having symptoms, will discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy (shock wave procedure to break up the stone) or ureteroscopy (using a small telescope/camera to go up to the urethra and bladder and up into the ureter to retrieve the stone).
- Contact the office if experiencing worsening symptoms.

REASON FOR VISIT: Nonhealing foot ulcer on the right foot.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: 
The patient is a male with diabetes and diabetic neuropathy who presents with a nonhealing right foot ulcer. He has been wearing a boot for about six weeks. The issue started when he put on a pair of new diabetic shoes and inserts that were a little bit too tight, felt burning and stinging, and looked down to see a blister on the pad of the bottom of his foot around his heel. He had been walking on the front part of his foot. He started to notice a foul smell, and his wife and dog also noticed the smell. They looked and saw the blister had become unroofed, revealing thick, soft, mushy skin with a bad smell and yellow drainage. 

His primary care doctor started him on antibiotics about six days ago (out of a 10-day course, currently on day 6 or 7). He reports no nausea or vomiting. His wife checked his temperature, which was 99.7, and he had chills at one point requiring an extra blanket in bed. When he started antibiotics, it started to feel pretty good, but he has now noticed it has turned black around the outside of the wound. He is getting cramping in his calf muscle, a red streak coming up the front part of his ankle along the inside portion of his calf muscle, and it is super hot. 

He reports the pain has progressed from initial stinging to a throbbing pain "like there is a fire poker in the bottom of his foot." The inside of his calf muscle is really hard, and every time he pushes it, he feels it all the way up to his knee behind his kneecap. Additionally, he has been coughing a lot the last two days and has had a difficult time catching his breath when walking around the house.

BLOOD SUGARS: 
His hemoglobin A1c is 6.7 and has been for about two years, and he rarely has blood sugars over 200, checking 2-3 times a day. However, his sugars have been trending in the 300s to 400s over the last two weeks, with one spike at 500 to 600.

ACTIVITIES: 
He went hiking at Charlie's Bunion about a week before the ulcer developed. He got a new pair of diabetic shoes and inserts, and the prosthetist told him to check his feet every day. He went hiking about the third or fourth day and feels he just went too far.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
- Vital signs: Slight fever recognized, otherwise vitals look good.
- Foot exam: Necrotic wound on the heel approximately 2 x 2 centimeters. Sloughing of tissue present. Cellulitis and erythema around the area. Foul odor appreciated. No bony exposure. 
- Vascular exam: Bilateral palpable femoral and popliteal pulses present. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses not palpable, but present via Doppler.
- Sensation: Patient does not feel pressure on the actual affected area of the wound.

DIAGNOSTIC RESULTS:
- Right foot X-ray performed today: No evidence of osteomyelitis (no infection of the bone).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
- Nonhealing diabetic foot ulcer.
- Order a test to check the blood supply for the wound.
- Perform an in-office debridement today.
- Obtain a wound culture.
- Continue current antibiotic therapy prescribed by the PCP (finish the 10-to-12-day course) and evaluate culture results to determine if antibiotic therapy needs to be changed or extended, given concerns about the redness moving up the leg, swelling, and calf pain.
- Closely monitor the wound and patient. Follow up in 7 days.
- Diabetes management: Follow up with endocrinologist to keep hemoglobin A1c below 7 and closely monitor blood sugars given upcoming medication therapy with antibiotics and potentially other medications.
